doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Jazz clubs and education in major cities
summary: Harris says jazz thrives where there is a legacy and argues schools must teach jazz so clubs can grow.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: That’s fabulous. Jazz seems to be doing quite well in the universities and through efforts of people like yourselves. Do you have a sense of the music in the club scene and that kind of venue? What’s the state of jazz in that realm?
In New Orleans or in the United States?
Well whatever you feel that you could address.

I think that in major cities where we know that there is a great jazz legacy it’s doing well. I mean if you look at Chicago, New York, probably Kansas and St. Louis, it’s doing well. I think in other cities no, because if people are not supporting the music, if they’re not playing it, if it’s not part of the educational system in those cities, well there’s obviously not a large number of musicians playing the music. I think that clubs are very important

because you know that’s where the music was really created, that’s where it was kind of nurtured. I think now in the United States we’re moving in another direction. I think now we’re educating young people at an earlier age about it. I also think though that I think school systems must incorporate jazz as part of its curriculum. And you know that doesn’t exist a whole lot in the United States. Kids are taught classical music but not very much jazz. I think that’s very important. And we don’t have to worry about the music of the time because young people always gravitate to that and they do play that. And you know they don’t have to know how to read music to play that. But I think that school systems must incorporate a curriculum for jazz music and as that happens then the night club scene will really grow and develop as well.
